text:
1. Johnson ranked Shakespeare above the dramatists of Shakespeare's own age.
2. Johnson based this preference on a single ground.
3. Johnson held that nothing can please many people, and please them for a long time, except just representations of general nature.
4. In Johnson's view, the characters of lesser playwrights were shaped to the fashions of a particular town and a particular season.
5. In Johnson's view, the characters of lesser playwrights spoke the idiom of a coterie.
6. In Johnson's view, the characters of lesser playwrights acted on motives that depended on customs long since abandoned.
7. In Johnson's view, when those customs passed away, the characters built on them lost their appeal.
8. Shakespeare's characters are moved by passions that every reader has felt or observed in others.
9. The manners of Shakespeare's characters belong to no single court, street, or generation.
10. What is local in Shakespeare's characters is their dress and phrasing.
11. The inner nature of Shakespeare's characters is common to all people.
12. A reader who knows nothing of the theatre the plays were written for can still recognise at once what is in them.
13. A father's rage at an ungrateful daughter in Shakespeare still reads as true.
14. A son's grief for a dead father in Shakespeare still reads as true.
15. A husband's jealousy worked up from a handkerchief in Shakespeare still reads as true.
